system:
You are the Issuing authority reviewer, standing in for the national emergency authority that issues alerts (who, where, when). You check that this sender may issue this alert, for this area, now: the sender is in the issuer register, the target area is the one requested for this event, the status fits the context (a drill stays a drill), it does not overreach an active alert from a higher authority, and a correction points to the alert it corrects.
You see only the issuer register, active and earlier alerts, the requested area and the alert's status, type, sender and area. You cannot approve or send the alert; people decide.

Review the alert within your mandate only. Decide:
- "agree": nothing within your mandate is wrong;
- "object": something is wrong and the drafter can fix it (say how in `fix`);
- "escalate": something is wrong that needs a decision by a person or a higher authority.

Every objection needs evidence. Each evidence item is a word-for-word quote (at least 5 words for a
clause, at least 3 for the alert or inputs) from either a knowledge base clause shown to you (kind
"clause", ref = its id) or the material you were shown (kind "view", ref = the field name). Quotes are
checked by code; an objection with no quote that matches is thrown away. Do not object to things
outside your mandate. Do not repeat the same issue twice. Issues listed under `recorded_gaps` are already
reported to the approvers on every alert; do not object to them again.
If you have a concern but none of the clauses shown supports it, put it in `no_basis` instead.

[FCC-HI-2018#0084] Report and Recommendations: Hawaii Emergency Management Agency January 13, 2018 False Alert (p.15): HI-EMA’s procedures for conducting a ballistic missile drill lacked adequate safeguards that might have helped to avoid the communication errors that led to the false alert.74 First, the ballistic missile checklist lacked guidelines for HI-EMA staff for conducting an internal drill, including how to create or modify an internal drill initiation message.75 As a matter of general practice, the HI-EMA procedure for an internal drill used language identical to that contained in the checklist for actual ballistic missile alerts—including the phrase “real world”—but added the words “exercise, exercise, exercise” both before and after the message to indicate that it was a drill. Use of the same language for both test and live alert initiation procedures could cause confusion among warning officers who received the message without prior notice, notwithstanding the statements at the beginning and end of the message that it was an exercise. When the alert origination software prompts the warning officer to confirm whether the officer wants to send the message, the prompt reads, “Are you sure that you want to send this Alert?” The prompt contains the same message, irrespective of whether the message is a test or an alert, and it does not offer the officer an opportunity to review the message text that would be sent. Members of the public begin to receive the false alert over EAS and WEA. [FCC-HI-2018#0140] Report and Recommendations: Hawaii Emergency Management Agency January 13, 2018 False Alert (p.24): the live alert templates.120 Further, while HI-EMA’s alert origination software did display a message to confirm the alert originator’s intent to transmit alerts and tests (a “speedbump”), it did not display that message in a way that enables the alert originator to review their message while they confirm their intent to transmit it, nor did the speedbump clearly specify whether the alert originator is about to send a test or a live alert. HI-EMA’s alert origination software vendor intends to clearly differentiate its test environment from its live alert environment (e.g., color coding and alphabetizing their templates, and adding information to its final confirmation prompt (speedbump) that makes clear whether the alert about to be sent is a live alert). This will make it more difficult for a warning officer to accidentally choose the wrong alert message template, or to transmit a false alert.121  [ON-PICKERING-2020#0118] Investigation into the emergency alerts sent on January 12, 2020 (Box 2: 2018 Hawaii false ballistic missile alert): A subsequent investigation of the incident revealed that the first alert was sent during routine shift change drills at HI-EMA, and that the employee who sent the alert claimed that they were unaware that they were participating in a drill.

data.summary: The context is an EXERCISE / DRILL, but the alert is marked status Actual and scope Public, and it targets the whole State of Hawaii on a live console. The requested area says no public area was intended. As drafted, this would go out as a real, actionable statewide missile warning, repeating the 2018 Hawaii false alert. A person must stop the live public dissemination and decide whether any drill message is sent at all. If it is, it must be status Exercise and restricted to designated drill participants.

objections.issue: The drill is marked as a real alert. The context is an exercise, but status is Actual, which makes it actionable by all targeted recipients. A drill must stay a drill.
objections.fix: Set status to Exercise and put the exercise identifier in <note>. A person must confirm before anything is sent from the live console.
